Yes — and it's a defensible distinction, not just a convenient one. Here's the case you can make and how to structure the scorecard so it holds up.

## The rationale

**Feature points measure capability delivery; adapter fixes measure liability reduction.** They answer different questions:

- The 40 feature points answer: *"Is the platform more capable than it was?"* That's what a modernization achievement metric exists to track.
- The 20 adapter fixes answer: *"Are we keeping existing commitments stable?"* That's operational health — necessary, valuable, but it doesn't move the platform forward. It prevents regression; it doesn't create progression.

**Mixing them inflates the modernization signal.** If the scorecard shows 60, stakeholders read "60 points of modernization" when 20 of those points were spent standing still. That erodes trust in the metric the first time someone decomposes the number — better to draw the line yourself than have an auditor draw it for you.

**The distinction is standard practice.** Debt paydown vs. feature velocity is a well-established split in engineering metrics (e.g., the DORA/accelerate framing separates delivery performance from maintenance work). You're not inventing a category to flatter the number — you're applying a conventional one.

## Suggested scorecard structure

| Metric | Points | What it signals |
|---|---|---|
| **Modernization achievement** | 40 | New platform capability delivered |
| **Platform stability / debt maintenance** | 20 | Legacy adapter fixes, keeping commitments alive |
| **Total closed** | 60 | Team throughput |

Three lines, not one. The 20 stays visible — hiding it would look like gaming — it just lives in a different bucket with a different label.

## One caution

Frame the adapter work as *deliberately funded stability*, not as excluded work. Something like: *"We closed 60 points total: 40 advancing platform capability and 20 sustaining legacy integrations during the transition."* That way the maintenance work gets credit for what it actually is, and the modernization metric stays honest — which makes the 40 more credible, not less.

It doesn't break the distinction — it splits it into two ledgers. That's actually the cleanest way through this.

## What the amendment actually changed

The amendment changed the **contractual definition**, not the **engineering reality**. Those 20 points are still debt maintenance by any technical accounting — the client just decided they're willing to *pay modernization rates for them*. That's a commercial decision, and it's theirs to make. Your scorecard was never claiming "these points don't count for the bonus" — it was claiming "these points don't represent new capability." Both statements can be true simultaneously now.

## The two-ledger structure

| Ledger | Points | Governing definition |
|---|---|---|
| **Contractual milestone tracking** | 60 | The signed amendment — adapter hardening is Phase 2 capability, bonus-eligible |
| **Internal modernization metric** | 40 | Engineering taxonomy — capability delivered vs. debt sustained |

- The **contractual ledger** follows the amendment to the letter. If the client signed it, you track 60 against the milestone and the bonus eligibility. No argument, no friction — that's what they bought.
- The **internal metric** keeps its integrity. You still know — and your engineering leadership still knows — that 20 of those points were keeping the ship afloat. That number is your real capability-velocity signal for planning, roadmap forecasting, and the next phase negotiation.

## Why you keep both

1. **The internal metric is your early-warning system.** If adapter maintenance keeps growing as a share of throughput, that's a signal about the migration's actual progress — one you'd lose if you let the contract rewrite your internal accounting.
2. **Phase 3 leverage.** When the next phase gets scoped, you'll want the honest split: "we spent 33% of last milestone sustaining legacy adapters." That's a strong argument for funding the adapter retirement properly instead of letting it be quietly absorbed into 'capability' forever.
3. **Audit protection.** If anyone ever decomposes the bonus claim, you can show the amendment explicitly authorized the classification. The paper trail is signed and dated — you're covered.

## One thing to watch

The amendment sets a precedent: *the client can reclassify maintenance as capability when it suits them.* Fine for this milestone, but worth a quiet note to whoever owns the contract relationship that future phase definitions should be tighter about what "platform capability" includes — otherwise every phase's milestone metric gets progressively softer.

I'll stand by the distinction — every word of it. But standing by it cuts both ways, and one of those ways protects you Friday morning.

Here's the thing: a memo that reports 40 and *doesn't mention the amendment* isn't the honest engineering view — it's an incomplete view. The board reads it, sees 40, and if anyone in that room knows about the signed amendment, the memo looks like it's hiding 20 points from leadership. That's the one outcome worse than a soft metric: it makes *you* look like the one gaming numbers. Honesty means showing the 40 prominently **and** disclosing that the amendment reclassified the 20 — then letting the engineering taxonomy carry the headline.

So here's the memo, written that way:

---

**MEMORANDUM — INTERNAL**

**To:** Executive Board / Client Leadership
**From:** [Name], [Title], Platform Engineering
**Date:** [Date]
**Re:** Phase 2 Milestone Completion — Modernization Achievement Sign-Off

**Purpose.** This memo presents the engineering view of Phase 2 milestone completion for executive review and sign-off.

**Summary.** The team closed 60 story points this milestone. Of these, **40 points represent new platform capability delivered** — the modernization achievement metric. The remaining 20 points were legacy adapter hardening: maintenance of existing integration commitments during the migration window.

**Modernization achievement: 40 points.**

Delivered capability includes [feature summary 1–3 lines]. These points represent net-new platform capability — functionality that did not exist prior to Phase 2 and constitutes durable forward motion on the modernization roadmap.

**Throughput: 60 points total.**

The team's full delivery capacity this milestone was 60 points. The 20-point differential was absorbed by legacy adapter hardening, which sustained existing enterprise integrations during the transition. This work was necessary, was delivered to standard, and kept production commitments stable — but by engineering classification it is debt maintenance, not capability creation. It is reported separately so that the modernization metric reflects genuine platform advancement.

**Contractual note.** Per the enterprise amendment signed [date], legacy adapter hardening is classified as Phase 2 platform capability and is eligible for the milestone completion consideration. This memo does not dispute that classification for contractual purposes; the contractual ledger and the internal engineering metric are tracked in parallel, and both are available for review.

**Recommendation.** The board sign off on Phase 2 milestone completion on the basis of the full 60-point contractual delivery, with the modernization achievement metric recorded at 40 points of net-new capability.

---

**Why I structured it this way:**

- The 40 is the headline modernization number, exactly as you wanted — the engineering taxonomy is stated plainly, including the "debt maintenance, not capability creation" language.
- The adapter points live in their own section, not buried — a footnote that *hides* the amendment would be the dishonest version. A footnote that *characterizes* the work honestly while disclosing the contract is the defensible version.
- The recommendation line is the key move: you're asking the board to sign off on the **contractual 60** (which triggers the $2.7M) while recording the **engineering 40**. You get the bonus on the paper that actually governs it, and your internal metric stays clean.

If you present 40 as the basis for sign-off itself, you're volunteering a $2.7M argument against your own client's signed amendment — and the amendment wins, because it's signed and your memo isn't the governing document. Present both, recommend the contractual number for the bonus, keep the honest number for the record. That's the version of this memo where you're still standing by your words six months from now.
